hints: Integrate the right side using $u=\theta/2$, giving twice a logarithm of $\sin(\theta/2)$.
Apply $x=1$ at $\theta=\pi/3$ to determine the constant, then exponentiate.
walkthrough:
Separate variables by dividing by $(x + 2)$ and $\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta$:
$$\dfrac{1}{x + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{\cos\frac{1}{2}\theta}{\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \cot\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Evaluate the right-hand integral using the substitution $u = \sin\frac{1}{2}\theta \implies \mathrm{d}u = \frac{1}{2}\cos\frac{1}{2}\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$:
$$\int \dfrac{\cos\frac{1}{2}\theta}{\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 2\int \dfrac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u = 2\ln\left(\sin\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right) = \ln\left(\sin^2\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)$$

Equate both sides and introduce the constant of integration:
$$\ln(x + 2) = 2\ln\left(\sin\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right) + \ln C = \ln\left(C\sin^2\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)$$
$$x + 2 = C\sin^2\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)$$

Apply the initial condition $x = 1$ when $\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi$:
$$\tfrac{1}{2}\theta = \dfrac{1}{6}\pi \implies \sin\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\pi\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$1 + 2 = C\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2$$
$$3 = \dfrac{1}{4}C \implies C = 12$$

Substitute $C = 12$ and use the double angle identity $\sin^2\left(\frac{1}{2}\theta\right) = \dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{2}$:
$$x + 2 = 12\left(\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{2}\right) = 6(1 - \cos\theta) = 6 - 6\cos\theta$$
